chunks.text: 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Data description We used 53 single-cell-resolution spatial transcriptomics datasets comprising 413,376 spatial cells or spots to validate and benchmark SpCAST. These datasets were generated by five spatial transcriptomics technologies, including seqFISH+ [ Eng2019SeqFISHPlus ] , MERFISH [ Chen2015MERFISH ] , CosMx SMI [ He2022SpatialMolecularImaging ] , Slide-tags [ Russell2025SlideTagsNRG ] and Xenium [ Janesick2023Xenium ] , and covered both imaging-based and sequencing-based platforms. The datasets represented diverse biological systems, including mouse brain tissues and human cancer tissues such as non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). For model evaluation and benchmarking, cell-type annotations provided by the original studies were used as benchmark reference labels. Corresponding scRNA-seq reference datasets were curated for cross-modal cell-type transfer, including datasets generated by droplet-based scRNA-seq platforms such as 10x Chromium and Drop-seq [ Zheng2017Chromium , Macosko2015DropSeq ] . 2.2 Data preprocessing All datasets were preprocessed using Scanpy [ Wolf2018Scanpy ] to ensure consistent handling of count matrices and preparation for spatial and single-cell integration. The preprocessing workflow included quality control, normalization, feature selection and cross-modality gene alignment. Normalization. For each dataset, raw count matrices were normalized to a total count of 10,000 per cell or spatial unit, followed by log1p transformation to stabilize variance across genes. scRNA-seq preprocessing. For scRNA-seq reference datasets, quality control was first performed to remove low-quality genes and cells. Genes expressed in fewer than three cells were excluded. Cells with fewer than 300 total counts or fewer than 600 detected genes were removed. Highly variable genes (HVGs) were then selected from the filtered expression matrix for downstream integration and model training. Spatial transcriptomics preprocessing.

Spatial transcriptomics datasets were processed using gene-level filtering and normalization procedures. Genes expressed in fewer than three spatial cells or spots were removed, followed by HVG selection. Because sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics technologies often produce highly sparse expression matrices, we applied a spatial data enhancement preprocessing step to sequencing-based datasets, including Slide-tags, to reduce sparsity before cross-modal integration, as described below. Dataset integration. For each spatial dataset and its corresponding scRNA-seq reference, shared genes across the two modalities were identified and used for alignment. After intersecting the gene sets, HVGs were selected from the shared genes, and the top 2,000 HVGs were retained as the final feature set for downstream model training. 2.3 Spatial data enhancement Sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics datasets often exhibit high sparsity in their gene expression matrices. To reduce sparsity while preserving local spatial structure, we applied a spatial data enhancement procedure that integrated spatial proximity with gene expression similarity. K-nearest neighbor graph construction. For each spatial cell or spot, its k k -nearest neighbors were identified based on two-dimensional spatial coordinates, resulting in a spatial proximity matrix 𝐀 \mathbf{A} . Expression similarity estimation. Gene expression profiles were first reduced using principal component analysis (PCA) [ Mackiewicz1993PCA ] . Pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients were then computed between spatial cells or spots based on the reduced expression profiles to estimate transcriptomic similarity [ Benesty2008Pearson ] , resulting in an expression similarity matrix 𝐑 \mathbf{R} . Combined coefficient matrix. The spatial proximity matrix and expression similarity matrix were multiplied element-wise to construct a combined coefficient matrix.

Negative correlation values were set to zero, and the resulting matrix was row-normalized to ensure comparable enhancement strength across spatial cells or spots: 𝐂 = RowNorm ⁡ [ 𝐀 ⊙ max ⁡ ( 𝐑 , 0 ) ] , \mathbf{C}=\operatorname{RowNorm}\left[\mathbf{A}\odot\max(\mathbf{R},0)\right], (1) where ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. Enhanced expression matrix. The enhanced expression matrix was computed as follows: 𝐗 ′ = 𝐗 + α ​ 𝐂𝐗 , \mathbf{X}^{\prime}=\mathbf{X}+\alpha\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}, (2) where 𝐗 \mathbf{X} denotes the original expression matrix, 𝐂 \mathbf{C} denotes the row-normalized combined coefficient matrix, and α \alpha denotes the enhancement coefficient controlling the contribution of the neighborhood-derived expression term. This procedure was applied only to sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics datasets to mitigate expression sparsity while preserving local spatial expression patterns. The default value of α \alpha was determined through an ablation study on Slide-tags cortex datasets, in which the enhancement module was either disabled or α \alpha was varied from 0.0 to 0.9. This analysis showed that α = 0.2 \alpha=0.2 yielded the best overall performance in terms of accuracy, weighted F1 score, weighted precision, and weighted recall across datasets and random seeds, whereas α = 0.0 \alpha=0.0 was equivalent to disabling the enhancement term (Supplementary Table S1 ). Accordingly, α = 0.2 \alpha=0.2 was adopted as the default enhancement coefficient for sequencing-based scST datasets. 2.4 Overview of SpCAST SpCAST addresses cell-type annotation in single-cell-resolution spatial transcriptomics (scST) as a reference-guided cross-modal transfer problem. Given an annotated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) reference and an unannotated scST query dataset, SpCAST learns to transfer cell-type information from reference transcriptomic profiles to spatially resolved molecular measurements while preserving spatial tissue context (Fig. 1 A).

After preprocessing and gene alignment, let 𝐗 sc ∈ ℝ N sc × G \mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{sc}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathrm{sc}}\times G} denote the scRNA-seq reference expression matrix and 𝐗 st ∈ ℝ N st × G \mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{st}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathrm{st}}\times G} denote the scST expression matrix defined on the same set of shared genes. Here, N sc N_{\mathrm{sc}} and N st N_{\mathrm{st}} denote the numbers of reference cells and spatial cells or spots, respectively, and G G denotes the number of shared genes. The reference annotations are represented as a one-hot label matrix 𝐘 sc ∈ { 0 , 1 } N sc × K \mathbf{Y}_{\mathrm{sc}}\in\{0,1\}^{N_{\mathrm{sc}}\times K} , where K K is the number of annotated cell types. SpCAST uses a Kolmogorov–Arnold network (KAN)-based encoder to map scRNA-seq and scST profiles into a shared latent space [ Liu2024KAN ] , producing latent representations 𝐇 sc \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{sc}} and 𝐇 st \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{st}} . Built on this shared representation, a classification branch transfers cell-type labels from the annotated scRNA-seq reference to spatial cells or spots, whereas a reconstruction branch decodes the spatial latent representation to generate reconstruction-aware spatial expression profiles. Gene-level contribution scores are further estimated from the trained model to support SHAP-based attribution, marker-gene candidate prioritization and downstream biological interpretation (Fig. 1 A). Figure 1: Overview of the SpCAST framework. (A) Schematic of the SpCAST workflow. Spatial single-cell data are represented by a spatial graph and paired with a cell-by-gene expression matrix, after which a shared encoding layer maps spatial and reference scRNA-seq profiles into aligned latent representations. Cell-type supervision from the scRNA-seq reference supports label transfer to spatial cells, while reconstruction-aware modeling preserves spatial gene-expression information.

(B) Representative downstream applications enabled by SpCAST, including characterization of spatial cell-type organization, cross-species integration, re-annotation of originally unlabeled cells, marker gene identification using cell-type-specific marker scores, and reconstruction of spatial gene-expression patterns from sparse observations. 2.5 Kolmogorov–Arnold network layer KANs are inspired by the Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem [ Liu2024KAN ] , which states that a multivariate continuous function can be represented by compositions of univariate functions: f ​ ( 𝐱 ) = ∑ q = 1 2 ​ n + 1 Φ q ​ ( ∑ p = 1 n ϕ q , p ​ ( x p ) ) , f(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{q=1}^{2n+1}\Phi_{q}\left(\sum_{p=1}^{n}\phi_{q,p}(x_{p})\right), (3) where 𝐱 = ( x 1 , … , x n ) \mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) , and ϕ q , p \phi_{q,p} and Φ q \Phi_{q} denote univariate functions. In SpCAST, KAN layers were used to model nonlinear transcriptomic relationships between scRNA-seq references and spatial transcriptomics measurements. Given an input vector 𝐡 ( l ) ∈ ℝ d l \mathbf{h}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{l}} , the output of a KAN layer is defined as: h j ( l + 1 ) = ∑ i = 1 d l φ j , i ( l ) ​ ( h i ( l ) ) , j = 1 , … , d l + 1 , h^{(l+1)}_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{d_{l}}\varphi^{(l)}_{j,i}\left(h^{(l)}_{i}\right),\quad j=1,\ldots,d_{l+1}, (4) where φ j , i ( l ) \varphi^{(l)}_{j,i} is a learnable edge function connecting input node i i to output node j j .

Each edge function is parameterized as: φ j , i ( l ) ​ ( x ) = w b , j , i ( l ) ​ b ​ ( x ) + w s , j , i ( l ) ​ ∑ r = 1 R c j , i , r ( l ) ​ B r ​ ( x ) , \varphi^{(l)}_{j,i}(x)=w^{(l)}_{b,j,i}b(x)+w^{(l)}_{s,j,i}\sum_{r=1}^{R}c^{(l)}_{j,i,r}B_{r}(x), (5) where b ​ ( x ) b(x) denotes a base activation function, B r ​ ( x ) B_{r}(x) denotes the r r -th B-spline basis function, c j , i , r ( l ) c^{(l)}_{j,i,r} denotes the spline coefficient, and w b , j , i ( l ) w^{(l)}_{b,j,i} and w s , j , i ( l ) w^{(l)}_{s,j,i} are learnable scaling parameters. This formulation enables SpCAST to model nonlinear gene-expression relationships, while the trained prediction function can be further analyzed using feature-attribution methods to relate cell-type predictions to input genes. 2.6 Training objective During training, SpCAST jointly optimizes labeled scRNA-seq reference cells and unlabeled scST cells or spots in mini-batches. The KAN-based encoder maps the two modalities into latent representations 𝐇 sc \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{sc}} and 𝐇 st \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{st}} , which are optimized to preserve cell-type-discriminative information from the annotated reference while reducing cross-modal distributional mismatch. Built on this shared latent space, the classification branch predicts cell-type probabilities, whereas the reconstruction branch decodes 𝐇 st \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{st}} to generate reconstruction-aware spatial expression profiles and improve robustness to sparse molecular capture and dropout. SpCAST was trained using a multi-component objective that combines cross-modal alignment, reference-supervised cell-type classification and spatial expression reconstruction. Modality alignment loss.

To reduce modality discrepancy between the scRNA-seq reference and spatial transcriptomics data, we used a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) loss [ Gretton2012MMD ] between their latent representations: ℒ MMD = ‖ 1 N sc ​ ∑ i = 1 N sc ψ ​ ( 𝐡 i sc ) − 1 N st ​ ∑ j = 1 N st ψ ​ ( 𝐡 j st ) ‖ ℋ 2 , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MMD}}=\left\|\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{sc}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{sc}}}\psi(\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{sc}}_{i})-\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{st}}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\mathrm{st}}}\psi(\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{st}}_{j})\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}, (6) where ψ ​ ( ⋅ ) \psi(\cdot) denotes the feature map associated with a reproducing kernel Hilbert space ℋ \mathcal{H} . In practice, the empirical MMD can be computed using a kernel function k ​ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) k(\cdot,\cdot) : ℒ MMD = \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MMD}}= 1 N sc 2 ​ ∑ i = 1 N sc ∑ i ′ = 1 N sc k ​ ( 𝐡 i sc , 𝐡 i ′ sc ) + 1 N st 2 ​ ∑ j = 1 N st ∑ j ′ = 1 N st k ​ ( 𝐡 j st , 𝐡 j ′ st ) \displaystyle\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{sc}}^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{sc}}}\sum_{i^{\prime}=1}^{N_{\mathrm{sc}}}k(\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{sc}}_{i},\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{sc}}_{i^{\prime}})+\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{st}}^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\mathrm{st}}}\sum_{j^{\prime}=1}^{N_{\mathrm{st}}}k(\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{st}}_{j},\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{st}}_{j^{\prime}}) (7) − 2 N sc ​ N st ​ ∑ i = 1 N sc ∑ j = 1 N st k ​ ( 𝐡 i sc , 𝐡 j st ) . \displaystyle-\frac{2}{N_{\mathrm{sc}}N_{\mathrm{st}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{sc}}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\mathrm{st}}}k(\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{sc}}_{i},\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{st}}_{j}). Classification loss. For cell-type label transfer, SpCAST uses the annotated scRNA-seq reference to train a classifier on the latent representation.

The classification loss is defined as: ℒ CE = − 1 N sc ​ ∑ i = 1 N sc ∑ k = 1 K y i , k sc ​ log ⁡ p i , k sc , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}=-\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{sc}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{sc}}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}y^{\mathrm{sc}}_{i,k}\log p^{\mathrm{sc}}_{i,k}, (8) where y i , k sc y^{\mathrm{sc}}_{i,k} is the one-hot label indicating whether scRNA-seq cell i i belongs to cell type k k , and p i , k sc p^{\mathrm{sc}}_{i,k} is the predicted probability for cell type k k . After training, the same classifier is applied to the spatial latent representation to obtain predicted cell-type probabilities for spatial cells or spots. Reconstruction loss. To encourage reconstruction-aware spatial expression modeling, SpCAST decodes the latent spatial representation into a reconstructed expression matrix 𝐗 ^ st \widehat{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathrm{st}} . The reconstruction loss is defined as: ℒ rec = 1 N st ​ G ​ ‖ 𝐗 ^ st − 𝐗 st ‖ F 2 , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{st}}G}\left\|\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathrm{st}}-\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{st}}\right\|_{F}^{2}, (9) where ∥ ⋅ ∥ F \|\cdot\|_{F} denotes the Frobenius norm. Total loss. The total training objective is: ℒ total = λ CE ​ ℒ CE + λ MMD ​ ℒ MMD + λ rec ​ ℒ rec . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{CE}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{MMD}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MMD}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{rec}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}. (10) In this study, the default loss weights were set to λ CE = 1.00 \lambda_{\mathrm{CE}}=1.00 , λ MMD = 0.03 \lambda_{\mathrm{MMD}}=0.03 and λ rec = 0.01 \lambda_{\mathrm{rec}}=0.01 . 2.7 Inference and output generation During inference, only the scST dataset is required as input.

For each spatial cell or spot j j , SpCAST outputs a cell-type probability vector 𝐩 j st = ( p j , 1 st , … , p j , K st ) , \mathbf{p}^{\mathrm{st}}_{j}=(p^{\mathrm{st}}_{j,1},\ldots,p^{\mathrm{st}}_{j,K}), where p j , k st p^{\mathrm{st}}_{j,k} denotes the predicted probability that spatial cell or spot j j belongs to cell type k k . The final cell-type label is assigned by maximum posterior probability: y ^ j st = arg ⁡ max k ∈ { 1 , … , K } ⁡ p j , k st . \widehat{y}^{\mathrm{st}}_{j}=\arg\max_{k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}p^{\mathrm{st}}_{j,k}. (11) In addition to predicted cell-type labels, the trained model outputs reconstruction-aware spatial expression profiles. Gene-level contribution scores are further estimated from the trained model to quantify the contribution of individual genes to cell-type prediction. These outputs support downstream analyses, including spatial organization analysis, cross-species transfer evaluation, QC-guided assignment of originally unlabeled cells, marker-gene candidate prioritization, and reconstruction-supported analysis of spatial marker coherence (Fig. 1 B). 2.8 Gene-level attribution and marker-gene candidate prioritization To prioritize genes associated with SpCAST cell-type predictions, we used SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to quantify the contribution of each input gene to model output [ LundbergLee2017SHAP ] . These attribution scores were used to identify marker-gene candidates supporting model predictions.

G ! ​ [ f k ​ ( S ∪ { g } ) − f k ​ ( S ) ] , \varphi_{g}^{(k)}(f,\mathbf{x})=\sum_{S\subseteq\mathcal{G}\setminus\{g\}}\frac{|S|!\left(G-|S|-1\right)!}{G!}\left[f_{k}(S\cup\{g\})-f_{k}(S)\right], (12) where 𝒢 \mathcal{G} denotes the set of input genes, G = | 𝒢 | G=|\mathcal{G}| , and S S denotes a subset of genes excluding gene g g . The SHAP value estimates the marginal contribution of gene g g to the prediction score for cell type k k across possible feature coalitions. For each predicted cell type, gene-level attribution scores were obtained by aggregating absolute SHAP values across cells assigned to that cell type: s g , k = 1 | ℐ k | ​ ∑ i ∈ ℐ k | φ g ( k ) ​ ( f , 𝐱 i ) | , s_{g,k}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left|\varphi_{g}^{(k)}(f,\mathbf{x}_{i})\right|, (13) where ℐ k \mathcal{I}_{k} denotes the set of cells assigned to predicted cell type k k . Genes with high s g , k s_{g,k} values were considered marker-gene candidates or marker-supporting features associated with the corresponding predicted cell type. 2.9 Benchmarking and baseline methods SpCAST was benchmarked against six representative spatial transcriptomics annotation methods, including cell2location [ Kleshchevnikov2022Cell2location ] , SPANN [ Yuan2024SPANN ] , Spatial-ID [ Shen2022SpatialID ] , Tangram [ Biancalani2021Tangram ] , STEM [ Hao2024STEM ] and SpatialScope [ Wan2023SpatialScope ] . All methods were evaluated on the same paired scRNA-seq reference and spatial transcriptomics datasets whenever applicable. For each dataset, the original cell-type annotations provided by the corresponding study were used as benchmark reference labels.

To evaluate model stability, experiments were repeated across multiple random seeds, and the resulting predictions and performance metrics were summarized across runs. 2.10 Performance evaluation SpCAST and baseline methods were evaluated using accuracy, weighted precision, weighted recall and weighted F1 score. For each spatial dataset, predicted labels were compared with the corresponding benchmark reference labels. 2.11 Runtime evaluation Runtime was evaluated to assess computational efficiency across datasets and methods. For each method and dataset, runtime was measured as wall-clock time for model training and inference under the same computing environment whenever applicable. For SpCAST, runtime included feature alignment, model training, spatial cell-type prediction and generation of reconstruction-aware expression outputs. Runtime values were summarized across datasets and compared with annotation performance to evaluate the trade-off between computational cost and predictive accuracy. 2.9 Benchmarking and baseline methods SpCAST was benchmarked against six representative spatial transcriptomics annotation methods, including cell2location [ Kleshchevnikov2022Cell2location ] , SPANN [ Yuan2024SPANN ] , Spatial-ID [ Shen2022SpatialID ] , Tangram [ Biancalani2021Tangram ] , STEM [ Hao2024STEM ] and SpatialScope [ Wan2023SpatialScope ] . (A) Seed-level stability analysis showing weighted F1 distributions across random seeds and dataset-level standard deviation for each method. (B) Rank-score comparison of SpCAST and baseline methods based on accuracy and weighted F1. For each dataset, metric values were averaged across three random seeds and converted into method-wise rank scores among the seven methods. Each dot represents one dataset-level rank score. (C) Dataset-level weighted F1 summary across 53 datasets spanning CosMx SMI, MERFISH, Slide-tags, seqFISH+ and Xenium. (D) Runtime distributions across spatial transcriptomics technologies and methods. Tangram was not included for Xenium datasets because it did not complete within the benchmark runtime and memory constraints. (E) Efficiency analysis comparing mean weighted F1 with mean wall-clock runtime for SpCAST and baseline methods. We first evaluated SpCAST in a comprehensive benchmark for robust cell-type annotation across scST technologies, tissue contexts and dataset scales. To ensure that the benchmark captured methodological diversity rather than a simple comparison with arbitrarily selected tools, we compared SpCAST with six representative baseline methods spanning major computational paradigms for reference-based spatial cell-type annotation and single-cell spatial transcriptomics (scST) integration, including cell2location [ Kleshchevnikov2022Cell2location ] , SPANN [ Yuan2024SPANN ] , Spatial-ID [ Shen2022SpatialID ] , Tangram [ Biancalani2021Tangram ] , STEM [ Hao2024STEM ] and SpatialScope [ Wan2023SpatialScope ] .

Specifically, cell2location represents probabilistic Bayesian cell-type mapping and deconvolution; Tangram represents a deep-learning-based spatial alignment framework that optimizes probabilistic single-cell-to-space mappings using shared gene-expression patterns; SPANN represents variational representation learning with prototype-based optimal transport and spatial regularization; Spatial-ID combines supervised transfer learning with spatial embedding; STEM learns spatially aware shared embeddings through deep transfer learning; and SpatialScope leverages deep generative modeling for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics integration. We evaluated annotation performance using complementary metrics: accuracy quantified the overall correctness of cell-type predictions, whereas weighted F1, weighted precision and weighted recall summarized class-wise performance while accounting for differences in cell-type abundance. Robustness to random initialization is essential for interpreting performance differences in multi-dataset benchmarks. The seed-level weighted F1 analysis showed that SpCAST produced consistent performance distributions across repeated runs and maintained low dataset-level standard deviation across seeds. In contrast, several baseline methods showed more pronounced seed-to-seed variability in a subset of datasets, with Spatial-ID displaying particularly large dataset-level variability in some cases. Similar trends were observed for accuracy, weighted precision and weighted recall, demonstrating stable annotation performance of SpCAST under independent random initializations (Fig. 2 A and Supplementary Fig. S1). After establishing seed-level stability, we examined dataset-level absolute performance to evaluate whether SpCAST generalized across heterogeneous spatial transcriptomics data types. The circular weighted F1 summary included 53 datasets across five technologies: CosMx SMI, MERFISH, Slide-tags, seqFISH+ and Xenium.

These platforms differ in molecular capture strategy, gene-panel design, tissue context and expression sparsity, providing a heterogeneous test of cross-platform annotation performance. Across this dataset-level summary, SpCAST maintained high weighted F1 values for most datasets and generally traced the outer performance envelope among the compared methods, indicating that its advantage was not confined to a single platform or a small subset of datasets. Similar dataset-level patterns were observed for accuracy, weighted precision and weighted recall (Fig. 2 C and Supplementary Fig. S2). We next compared SpCAST with baseline methods from the perspectives of relative performance and rank-based aggregation. In the rank-score analysis based on accuracy and weighted F1, SpCAST achieved the highest mean rank scores among all evaluated methods and remained clearly separated from the stronger baseline methods in weighted F1. To further characterize method-specific differences at the dataset level, we calculated performance deltas between SpCAST and each baseline and summarized the corresponding win rates across metrics. The delta analyses showed predominantly positive differences for SpCAST relative to most baselines in accuracy, weighted precision and weighted recall. The win-rate summary showed that SpCAST exceeded Tangram and STEM across all evaluated metrics and maintained high, metric-dependent win rates against cell2location, SPANN, Spatial-ID and SpatialScope. Together, these rank-score, delta and win-rate analyses indicate that the overall performance of SpCAST was not driven by a single metric or a small subset of datasets, but was observed across multiple baselines, datasets and evaluation criteria (Fig. 2 B and Supplementary Figs. S1 and S2). In addition to annotation accuracy, computational efficiency is an important practical criterion for applying cell-type annotation methods to large-scale scST datasets.

This consideration is becoming increasingly important as high-throughput spatial platforms with single-cell resolution, such as Xenium, now generate datasets containing hundreds of thousands of cells from a single tissue section. At this scale, computational efficiency affects not only runtime but also whether an annotation method can complete the analysis within available memory. We therefore measured the wall-clock runtime of each method under a unified benchmarking environment to assess the practical computational cost of the complete annotation pipeline. Runtime distributions varied across scST technologies, consistent with differences in platform-specific gene panels, cell numbers and data sparsity. When average weighted F1 was jointly considered with average runtime, SpCAST occupied the high-performance and low-runtime region, whereas several baseline methods required substantially longer runtime to achieve comparable or lower annotation performance. In contrast, Tangram and STEM showed lower mean weighted F1 or less favorable efficiency positions in this benchmark. Moreover, on larger Xenium datasets, methods that rely on explicit single-cell-to-space mapping matrices can become memory-limited, whereas SpCAST successfully completed the analysis, further demonstrating its scalability and practical utility for large-scale scST analysis. These results indicate that SpCAST provides practical pipeline-level computational efficiency in the evaluated benchmark setting while maintaining robust annotation performance (Fig. 2 D and E). 3.2 SpCAST recapitulates laminar excitatory neuron organization Beyond global benchmark performance, spatial annotation methods should preserve biological spatial patterns in tissues with defined organization.

We therefore evaluated SpCAST in mouse visual cortex seqFISH+ data, where cortical laminar architecture and excitatory neuron subtypes are well characterized [ Eng2019SeqFISHPlus , Tasic2016MouseV1Taxonomy , Tasic2018NeocorticalAreas , Belgard2011NeocorticalLayers , Yao2021IsocortexHPF ] . This dataset therefore represents a stringent evaluation setting, as excitatory L2/3, L4 and L5/6 neurons are transcriptionally related and spatially adjacent across cortical layers, making subtype-level separation a major source of annotation uncertainty. Consistent with this challenge, overall accuracies remained moderate across methods. Nevertheless, SpCAST achieved the highest accuracy, reaching 0.690 compared with 0.630 for cell2location, 0.620 for SpatialScope and 0.533 for SPANN (Fig. 3 A), whereas STEM, Spatial-ID and Tangram showed lower accuracies in the supplementary comparison (Supplementary Fig. S3). Label-transition analysis and complete confusion matrices further showed that the remaining errors of SpCAST were largely confined to related excitatory subtypes, rather than broadly distributed across unrelated cell classes (Fig. 3 E and Supplementary Fig. S5). Figure 3: SpCAST recapitulates marker-supported laminar excitatory neuron organization in mouse visual cortex seqFISH+ data. To evaluate SpCAST in this more challenging setting, we used Slide-tags data to construct a species-matched reference-transfer comparison and a mouse-to-human cross-species transfer analysis [ Russell2024SlideTagsNature ] . In the species-matched human-reference transfer, a human prefrontal cortex snRNA-seq reference was used to annotate the human scST query [ Herring2022HumanPFC ] ; in the mouse-to-human cross-species transfer, a mouse prefrontal cortex scRNA-seq reference was used to annotate the same human scST query [ Bhattacherjee2019MousePFC ] . Compared with species-matched reference transfer, cross-species transfer is affected by both technical differences between scRNA-seq and scST data and biological differences in gene content, ortholog mapping, cell-type taxonomy and species-specific expression programs [ Park2024SpeciesAgnostic , Zhang2025Icebear ] . The human and mouse datasets contained 13,281 orthologous genes, whereas 15,287 human genes and 6,236 mouse genes had no matched orthologs in the opposite species, indicating that this task was performed in a substantially restricted orthologous feature space.

Thus, this analysis was not intended to establish universal cross-species annotation capability, but rather to test whether SpCAST could maintain stable label-transfer performance in an ortholog-constrained Slide-tags mouse-to-human transfer setting (Fig. 4 C). Several methods achieved high annotation accuracy in this task, indicating relatively stable label transfer when the cell-type taxonomy and gene feature space were largely matched.

The Sankey diagrams showed that SpCAST retained more stable major cell-type correspondences between species-matched transfer and mouse-to-human transfer, with most cross-species flows remaining aligned with the corresponding ground-truth cell types. In contrast, several baseline methods exhibited more dispersed label transitions or stronger cross-class shifts under mouse-to-human transfer.

Supplementary precision and weighted F1 drop analyses further showed smaller performance changes for SpCAST across major cell classes, whereas several baselines exhibited pronounced degradation for specific cell types. Embedding-space error analysis showed that the error rate of SpCAST increased only slightly, from 2.5% in species-matched transfer to 2.9% in mouse-to-human transfer, whereas cell2location and Spatial-ID showed substantially larger cross-species error rates. Complete confusion matrices further indicated that SpCAST preserved clearer correspondences among major cell types under mouse-to-human transfer. S6–S8). 3.4 SpCAST prioritizes candidate identities for unlabeled Xenium cells Spatial annotation workflows often leave a subset of cells without reliable labels, particularly when transcript counts are low, marker evidence is ambiguous or cells reside in complex tumor microenvironments. We used a public human breast cancer Xenium dataset to test whether SpCAST could distinguish low-signal unlabeled cells from analyzable unlabeled cells and provide marker-supported candidate identities for the latter [ Janesick2023Xenium ] . Breast cancer tissues contain complex epithelial, stromal, immune, vascular and tumor-associated cellular compartments, providing a challenging context for candidate assignment of difficult-to-annotate cells [ Wu2021BreastCancerAtlas , Kumar2023HumanBreastAtlas , Reed2024HumanBreastCellAtlas , Jackson2020BreastPathologyLandscape , Nguyen2018BreastEpithelial , BhatNakshatri2021HealthyBreast , Xu2024BreastTumorAtlas ] . In this dataset, 8,554 of 167,780 cells were labeled as Unlabeled, representing 5.1% of all cells (Fig. 5 A,B).

After transcript-signal quality control, 4,573 originally Unlabeled cells were retained for downstream candidate-label assignment, corresponding to 53.5% of the original Unlabeled population; the remaining 3,981 low-signal cells were excluded from downstream label assignment to avoid over-interpreting cells with insufficient transcript evidence (Supplementary Fig. S9). Before assigning candidate identities to originally Unlabeled cells, we first evaluated each method on cells with existing labels to establish whether the Xenium dataset contained sufficient reference signal for label transfer. This task was non-trivial because breast cancer tissues include multiple cellular states and tumor-microenvironment compartments that can produce related or partially overlapping transcriptional profiles [ Wu2021BreastCancerAtlas , Azizi2018BreastImmuneMap , Jackson2020BreastPathologyLandscape ] . In the non-Unlabeled subset, SpCAST achieved an accuracy of 0.659, exceeding cell2location and slightly outperforming SpatialScope and Spatial-ID, which reached 0.280, 0.639 and 0.630, respectively (Fig. 5 A,B). STEM and SPANN showed lower accuracies in the supplementary comparison (Supplementary Fig. S10). Spatial maps and UMAP visualizations indicated that SpCAST better preserved the major cell-type spatial distributions and embedding structure than several baseline methods, supporting its use for candidate assignment of QC-passed originally Unlabeled cells. The dataset included astrocytes, inhibitory neurons, mature oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, mural cells, immature oligodendrocytes, excitatory neurons, microglia and ependymal cells. SpCAST retained the overall structure of these major cell populations in both spatial coordinates and UMAP representations [ McInnes2018UMAP ] , providing the basis for subsequent analysis of cell-type-associated marker scores (Fig. 6 A,B,E). This analysis was performed using a human non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) CosMx SMI dataset, which provides spatially resolved tumor-microenvironment information and cell-type distributions spanning tumor, fibroblast, immune, endothelial and epithelial compartments [ He2022SpatialMolecularImaging , Lambrechts2018LungTME , Travaglini2020HumanLungAtlas , Sikkema2023IntegratedLungAtlas , Salcher2022NSCLCAtlas , Luo2022PanCancerCAF , Lavie2022CAFSingleCellEra ] . Because the spatial organization of tumor, stromal and immune compartments is closely linked to tumor-microenvironment structure in NSCLC, this dataset provides a suitable context for evaluating whether reconstructed marker signals are more concordant with the corresponding cell-type regions. Spatial maps and UMAP visualizations first showed that SpCAST preserved the major cell-type organization and embedding structure in the CosMx SMI dataset, providing spatial references for downstream marker–cell-type concordance analysis (Fig. 7 A,B).

In particular, tumor and fibroblast cells formed recognizable spatial domains in the tissue, enabling evaluation of tumor-associated and fibroblast-associated marker genes against their corresponding cell-type spatial references [ He2022SpatialMolecularImaging , Lambrechts2018LungTME , DeZuani2024NSCLCSpatialSingleCell , Wu2021NSCLCHeterogeneity , Salcher2022NSCLCAtlas , Luo2022PanCancerCAF , Chen2023POSTNCAFNSCLC , Lavie2022CAFSingleCellEra ] . Comparison of original and reconstructed expression showed that SpCAST reconstruction increased the spatial continuity of representative marker signals and improved their concordance with the corresponding cell-type regions. For tumor-associated marker genes, the Spearman similarities between original expression and the tumor spatial reference were 0.087 for KRT6B and 0.030 for CEACAM6 ; after reconstruction, these values increased to 0.530 and 0.424, respectively. For the fibroblast-associated marker LUM , similarity increased from 0.150 in the original expression to 0.311 after reconstruction (Fig. 7 C). Spatial maps showed that the original marker signals were sparse and fragmented, whereas reconstructed expression patterns more closely followed the tumor or fibroblast spatial domains. These results indicate that SpCAST reconstruction provides information beyond discrete cell-type labels by improving the spatial concordance between marker expression and tissue organization. To test whether this improvement was limited to a few example genes, we further summarized gene-level spatial similarity across multiple tumor-associated and fibroblast-associated marker genes. In addition to KRT6B , CEACAM6 and LUM shown in the main spatial maps, KRT5 , KRT18 , KRT19 , EPCAM and DCN also showed higher spatial similarity after reconstruction (Supplementary Fig. S15) [ Cao2021ExosomalMarkersNSCLC , Luo2022PanCancerCAF , Chen2023POSTNCAFNSCLC , Xiao2025NSCLCFAPFibroblast , Lavie2022CAFSingleCellEra ] .

The gene-level summary showed increased marker–cell-type spatial similarity for all evaluated markers, with larger gains for several tumor-associated genes and more modest but directionally consistent improvement for fibroblast-associated genes (Fig. 7 D). This gene-specific pattern suggests that SpCAST reconstruction did not simply apply uniform smoothing to all expression fields; instead, it improved marker–cell-type spatial concordance in a gene-dependent manner across multiple marker genes. Because the spatial organization of tumor epithelial and stromal compartments is central to interpreting the NSCLC tumor microenvironment, these results suggest that reconstruction-aware spatial expression modeling in SpCAST can provide a complementary analysis beyond cell-type annotation [ Lambrechts2018LungTME , Travaglini2020HumanLungAtlas , Sikkema2023IntegratedLungAtlas , Qian2020PanCancerTME , DeZuani2024NSCLCSpatialSingleCell , Salcher2022NSCLCAtlas , Luo2022PanCancerCAF , Chen2023POSTNCAFNSCLC , Lavie2022CAFSingleCellEra ] . Overall, the CosMx SMI analysis supports the ability of SpCAST reconstruction to enhance spatial coherence in sparse or locally fragmented marker expression. This conclusion should be interpreted specifically as an improvement in marker–cell-type spatial concordance, rather than as direct validation that reconstructed expression recovers the unobserved true expression field. 4 Discussion In this study, we developed SpCAST, a Kolmogorov–Arnold network (KAN)-based framework for reference-guided analysis of single-cell-resolution spatial transcriptomics (scST) data [ Liu2024KAN ] . The main contribution of SpCAST is the integration of cell-type label transfer, gene-level attribution evidence and reconstruction-supported spatial marker analysis within a single model.

Compared with workflows that only output discrete cell-type labels or treat annotation, interpretation and expression reconstruction as separate steps, SpCAST provides an integrated framework in which predicted cell identities, gene features supporting those predictions and the concordance between marker expression and cell-type spatial domains can be evaluated together. The methodological design of SpCAST combines nonlinear cross-modal representation learning, distribution alignment, supervised label transfer and expression reconstruction. The KAN-based encoder models nonlinear correspondences between scRNA-seq reference profiles and scST measurements, whereas the MMD-based alignment and supervised classification objectives reduce cross-modal distributional mismatch while preserving cell-type-discriminative information from the annotated reference [ Gretton2012MMD ] . The reconstruction-aware objective further provides reconstructed spatial expression representations for downstream marker–cell-type spatial concordance analysis. By combining the trained nonlinear prediction function with SHAP-based attribution, SpCAST links model outputs to input-feature contributions and provides model-associated evidence for marker-gene candidate prioritization [ LundbergLee2017SHAP ] . Across 53 publicly available datasets comprising 413,376 spatial cells or spots and spanning five spatial transcriptomics technologies, SpCAST achieved competitive or improved annotation performance in the evaluated benchmark setting while maintaining favorable computational efficiency. Crucially, this performance extended beyond aggregate metrics; SpCAST demonstrated consistent stability across imaging-based and sequencing-based platforms, different gene panels, diverse tissue contexts and varying dataset scales.

As high-throughput single-cell-resolution spatial platforms such as Xenium and CosMx SMI continue to generate increasingly large datasets, runtime efficiency and memory scalability have become increasingly important practical requirements for spatial annotation methods [ Janesick2023Xenium , He2022SpatialMolecularImaging ] . Beyond global benchmarking, the case studies further demonstrated the biological utility of SpCAST in complex tissue analysis. In mouse visual cortex data, SpCAST better preserved the laminar organization of excitatory neuron subtypes and showed concordance with spatial expression patterns of known subtype-associated marker genes [ Eng2019SeqFISHPlus , Tasic2016MouseV1Taxonomy , Tasic2018NeocorticalAreas , Belgard2011NeocorticalLayers ] . When evaluated in an ortholog-constrained mouse-to-human transfer setting using Slide-tags data, SpCAST maintained relatively stable label-transfer performance, providing a concrete example for exploring conserved cellular organization across species [ Russell2024SlideTagsNature , Romero2012GeneExpressionEvolution , Hodge2019HumanMouseCortex ] . Furthermore, applied to human breast cancer Xenium data, SpCAST stratified originally Unlabeled cells into low-signal and QC-passed analyzable populations, providing marker-supported candidate identities for the latter [ Janesick2023Xenium , Wu2021BreastCancerAtlas , Kumar2023HumanBreastAtlas , Jackson2020BreastPathologyLandscape ] .
